title: Reproduction & Disability Ethics
rootClaim: Prospective parents have an absolute reproductive right to conceive children regardless of genetic disability, and state or social coercion restricting disabled reproduction is un-ethical.

branches.text: Reproductive Autonomy & Expressivist Objection: Restricting reproduction or selectively aborting for disability sends a devaluing message that living with a disability renders life not worth living.

children.text: Social Model of Disability: Disability is primarily created by unaccommodating societal structures and systemic prejudice rather than inherent medical impairment.
Medical Model Realism: Certain severe genetic conditions inflict intrinsic physical pain and organ failure independent of social accommodations or environmental accessibility.

Non-Identity Problem (Parfit): A child born with a disability cannot be said to have been harmed by being brought into existence, provided their life is worth living, because alternative selection would yield a different child.

Procreative Beneficence Principle (Savulescu): Parents hold a moral obligation to select the child, of the children they could have, who is expected to have the best life based on relevant genetic data.
Eugenic Slippery Slope: Institutionalizing genetic screening mandates or social pressure to avoid disability risks reviving dark historical eugenic practices and state coercion.

branches.text: Harm Prevention & Procreative Responsibility: Intentionally bringing a child into the world with a foreseeable severe suffering condition violates parental duty of care.

children.text: Child Welfare Maximization: Parents should minimize predictable chronic suffering and medical burden for prospective offspring whenever reproductive technology (e.g., PGD) is available.

Ableist Quality-of-Life Misconception: Empirical psychological studies show disabled individuals report subjective happiness and life satisfaction comparable to non-disabled peers (disability paradox).

definitions.description: Derek Parfit's philosophical puzzle concerning actions that affect who will exist in the future, making it difficult to claim a person was 'harmed' by being born with a condition if they would otherwise not exist.
Julian Savulescu's thesis that moral agents should choose to have the child who will have the best chance of the best life.
The perspective that disability is caused by the way society is organized, rather than by a person's impairment or difference.
The observation that patients with severe and persistent disabilities often report a good or excellent quality of life, contrary to public perception.
The argument that selecting against fetuses with disabilities sends a hurtful message that disabled lives are less valuable.
